title: Flour Weight: Why 1 Cup Is 120–160 g Depending on Scoop
h1: Flour by cup vs by gram — the 33% variance that breaks baking
description: 1 cup of all-purpose flour weighs 120 g spooned or 160 g scooped. Recipe failures traced to volume vs weight. Full weight table for wheat, bread, cake, whole-grain, and gluten-free flours.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against King Arthur Baking, USDA FoodData Central, and Serious Eats reference tests

hero: Scoop-and-shake fills a cup with 160 g of flour. Spoon-and-level fills the same cup with 120 g. Same measuring cup, same flour, 33% more mass in one — the single largest source of baking failures that get blamed on 'bad recipes' or 'the oven'.
body: Flour is compressible. Its bulk density depends on how much air is trapped between particles, which depends entirely on technique. This is why every serious baking book published since 2010 quotes gram weights: it removes the technique variable. King Arthur's standard is 120 g per cup for all-purpose flour, but 'the internet' averages 140 g because scoop-and-shake is more common than spoon-and-level.
## Reference weights per US cup

| Flour | Spooned (g) | Scooped (g) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| All-purpose (AP) | 120 | 160 | King Arthur standard 120 |
| Bread flour | 120 | 165 | Slightly denser, higher protein |
| Cake flour | 114 | 155 | Finer particle, packs tighter |
| Pastry flour | 113 | 150 | Between AP and cake |
| Whole wheat | 128 | 170 | Bran adds mass |
| Whole wheat pastry | 120 | 160 | Finer grind of whole wheat |
| Rye | 102 | 145 | Very low gluten, loose pack |
| Semolina | 168 | 200 | Coarser, denser |
| Almond flour | 96 | 120 | Fat content lowers density |
| Coconut flour | 112 | 150 | Absorbs water aggressively |
| Rice flour | 158 | 190 | Fine rice, packs dense |
| Buckwheat | 120 | 155 | Similar to AP |
| Chickpea (besan) | 92 | 130 | Very light |
| GF 1:1 blend | 140 | 170 | Bob's Red Mill, King Arthur |
## Why volume fails specifically for flour

Wheat kernels are milled into particles of ~10–100 μm. Loose-packed, they trap ~40% air by volume. Compacted (by scoop-and-shake, by tapping the cup, by settling during shipping), the air drops to ~25%. Same cup volume, different mass. Sugar is crystalline and does not compress this way — a cup of granulated sugar is 200 g whether you spoon or scoop. Flour is uniquely bad.
## Worked example — the failing cookie recipe
A chocolate chip cookie recipe calling for '2 cups AP flour' at the King Arthur standard is 240 g. Same recipe with scoop-and-shake gives 320 g — 33% more. The cookies:
- **240 g flour (correct):** spread wide, thin, crisp edges, chewy centre.
- **320 g flour (over-scooped):** stay in tight balls, cakey, pale, dry.
This is the number one 'why did my cookies fail' cause. Weigh the flour.
## Spoon-and-level, correctly

The King Arthur method: fluff the flour in the container with a whisk or fork. Spoon it into the measuring cup lightly — do not tap. Level off with a straight edge (back of a knife, scraper). Result: 120 g ± 3 g reliably. Total time: 15 seconds per cup, once you have the habit.
## Weight is faster than volume anyway

The stopwatch test: weighing 500 g of flour on a $15 kitchen scale takes 8 seconds (tare bowl, pour until display reads 500). Cup-measuring 500 g takes ~35 seconds (four cups spooned-and-levelled, one measured, more cleaning). Weight is faster and always accurate. The only reason cups persist in US home recipes is inertia.
## Baker's percentage — flour as reference

Professional bakeries use baker's percentage: flour = 100%, every other ingredient expressed as % of flour weight. A '70% hydration' ciabatta is 700 g water per 1000 g flour. A '2% salt' bread is 20 g salt per 1000 g flour. This scaling works flawlessly — but only if flour is measured by weight.
## When cups are safe

Small volumes of liquids (water, milk, oil) — a 5% cup error is invisible. Chopped vegetables, herbs, nuts — cup measurements are already approximations. Whole spices ground to taste. Everything else in a baked good: weigh.
## The special case of cake flour

Cake flour is often 'sifted, then measured' in older recipes; modern recipes say 'measure, then sift'. The difference is 15 g per cup (100 sifted vs 115 unsifted). If the recipe does not specify, and it is from before 2000, assume sifted-first (lighter). If after 2010, measure-first is the norm.
## The five-second recap

1 cup AP flour = 120 g if spooned, 160 g if scooped. Weigh in grams; it is faster and always right. If a recipe gives only cups, treat 120 g as the intended value unless the author explicitly says 'scoop-and-shake'.

faqs.q: What is one cup of AP flour in grams?
faqs.a: 120 g by the King Arthur / America's Test Kitchen standard (spooned and levelled). Older recipes and internet averages skew higher (140 g); scoop-and-shake reaches 160 g.
A little. Gold Medal AP is ~127 g/cup spooned. King Arthur is 120 g. Bob's Red Mill 1:1 GF is 140 g. Differences under 10% within a category; keep to one brand for consistency.

faqs.q: Can I convert an old cup-based recipe to grams once and reuse?
faqs.a: Yes. Convert once using 120 g per cup for wheat flours, then annotate the recipe. All future bakes are repeatable — no more 'this recipe used to work'.

faqs.q: Why do European recipes use grams by default?
faqs.a: European kitchens have kept scales as standard equipment; US kitchens phased them out mid-20th century in favour of nested measuring cups. Cultural, not technical.

faqs.q: What about volume for very small amounts?
faqs.a: Under 2 tsp (10 g flour range), a scale reads unreliably at 1 g resolution. Teaspoons are fine for tiny quantities — the percentage error at absolute mass is small.
